hints: Think about what a free-living alga in seawater might run short of for photosynthesis, and what is always being made inside a living animal cell that respires.
Link that extra supply to a named limiting factor and to the part of photosynthesis that uses it - the light independent reaction.
walkthrough:
What the alga gains from living inside an animal**
Living inside means sitting right next to mitochondria that are respiring all the time. Aerobic respiration releases carbon dioxide, plus heat and mineral ions from metabolism, so the alga is bathed in a much higher concentration than in open seawater where carbon dioxide diffuses slowly.

Why more carbon dioxide means faster photosynthesis**
Carbon dioxide is a raw material for the Calvin cycle, the light independent stage that makes triose phosphate. When carbon dioxide is in short supply it limits the rate. Inside the polyp it is not limiting, so the Calvin cycle can turn faster and the overall photosynthetic rate is higher than in free-living algae.

Final answer: Inside polyp cells algae receive a higher / non-limiting supply of carbon dioxide (and temperature / mineral ions) from polyp respiration / metabolism for use in the Calvin cycle / light independent reactions, increasing the rate of photosynthesis.

hints: Start by thinking how you can separate a mixture of coloured pigments that have different solubilities in the same solvent.
Picture the set-up - where you place a tiny concentrated spot of extract so it does not wash away, and how the solvent should move.
Think what two distances you must measure once the spots have separated to get a number for each pigment.
Recall the formula that turns those distances into an $R_f$ value and how known values let you name each pigment.
walkthrough:
Choose chromatography and apply a concentrated spot**
Paper or thin layer chromatography separates pigments because they differ in solubility in the solvent and attraction to the paper. Draw a pencil baseline near the base, spot on a tiny drop of algal extract, let it dry and repeat several times so you get a small dark concentrated spot that will give clear bands.

Run the chromatogram correctly**
Stand the paper upright in a tank with a suitable organic solvent, making sure the baseline spot is above the solvent level so it is not dissolved away. The solvent moves up by capillary action and carries the more soluble pigments further, separating chlorophyll a, peridinin, chlorophyll c2, dinoxanthin and beta-carotene into different spots.

Measure and calculate $R_f$**
When the solvent front is near the top, mark its position and the centre of each pigment spot. Measure distance travelled by pigment and distance travelled by solvent front from the baseline. For each spot calculate $$R_f = \frac{\text{distance travelled by pigment}}{\text{distance travelled by solvent front}}$$

Identify the pigments**
Each pigment has a characteristic $R_f$ in a given solvent system. Compare your calculated values with published known $R_f$ values to identify which spot is chlorophyll a, peridinin and the others, and relative size / intensity gives an idea of relative abundance.

Final answer: Separate by paper / thin layer chromatography; place a spot of pigment extract on the pencil baseline and dry and re-spot to concentrate; stand in solvent with spot above solvent level so solvent moves up; measure distance moved by each pigment and by solvent front, calculate $R_f = \frac{\text{distance by pigment}}{\text{distance by solvent front}}$ and compare with known $R_f$ values to identify.

hints: Look across Table 2.2 and count how many of the 10 absorption peaks fall inside the lamp range of 400-490 nm.
Check Table 2.1 to see which two pigments dominate the mixture and where their peaks lie.
Connect the chain - more of the right wavelengths absorbed means what for algal photosynthesis and then for the coral polyp that receives its products.
walkthrough:
Match the lamp to the absorption peaks**
The lamps give mostly 400-490 nm violet-blue light. In Table 2.2 almost every pigment has at least one peak in that band - chlorophyll a 430 nm, peridinin 456 and 485 nm, chlorophyll c2 450 and 396 nm, dinoxanthin 442 and 471 nm, beta-carotene 454 and 480 nm. That is 8 out of 10 peaks, so the lamp output is absorbed very well.

Weight by abundance**
Table 2.1 shows chlorophyll a 39% and peridinin 39% together make 78% of total pigment. Both have strong violet-blue absorption, so the bulk of the light-harvesting system is tuned to the lamp wavelengths. That makes these two pigments the most important for capturing lamp light.

From absorption to coral growth**
More photons absorbed means a higher rate of light dependent reactions and therefore more ATP and reduced NADP for the Calvin cycle, so algal photosynthesis rises. The algae pass excess carbohydrate / photosynthate to the coral polyps, providing energy and materials for respiration and biosynthesis, so coral growth increases.

Final answer: Most pigments absorb strongly in violet-blue 400-490 nm, 8 out of 10 peaks; chlorophyll a and peridinin are most abundant at 39% each and absorb well in this range; more light absorbed increases algal photosynthesis, supplying more product to the coral and increasing coral growth.
